questions.text: We can state in one sentence which entrepreneurs we serve, what problem we help them solve and what should change for them.
We have a written theory of change that links our activities to the results we expect for entrepreneurs.
We have tested at least one assumption in our theory of change against our own data and changed the programme as a result.
Most enterprises we supported in the last twelve months fit the target segment in our written mission or strategy.
Our curriculum and support are adapted to the sectors, languages and business conditions of the enterprises we serve, not imported unchanged.
We chose our programme length, cohort size and support intensity deliberately for the enterprises we serve, and can explain why.
Our programme design includes scheduled peer learning among entrepreneurs in the same cohort.
We design new programmes around what target entrepreneurs tell us they need, not only around what funders offer to pay for.
We know which other organisations serve the same enterprises in our area and how our offer differs from theirs.
We have an estimate of how many enterprises fit our target segment in our area and the share of them we reach each year.
We have a written strategic plan with measurable targets that leaders review at least once a year.
Our programme delivery model is written down well enough that a trained new team or a new location could run it.
Before adding cohorts, locations or programmes, we check that we have enough staff, mentors and funding to keep quality.
We select enterprises using written criteria that at least two reviewers score independently.
We keep a record of every applicant at every stage, with the reason for each selection or rejection.
We can show that we reach entrepreneurs who would not otherwise be supported, not only those already funded or well connected.
Each selected enterprise receives a baseline diagnostic that leads to a written support plan within 30 days of starting.
Most of our support time goes to the needs entrepreneurs rank highest, such as sales, finance access or hiring, not mainly to pitch preparation.
Entrepreneur feedback on mentors and sessions leads to documented changes in how we deliver.
Each entrepreneur is matched to a mentor or coach using a written view of the entrepreneur's needs and the mentor's expertise.
Market access support, such as buyer introductions or market information, is a deliberate part of our offer with named activities.
We have written criteria and a process for graduating, pausing or exiting enterprises from our programmes.
We were in contact with most alumni of our last three cohorts during the past twelve months.
After the programme ends, alumni have a defined follow-up offer, such as clinics, mentor access or investor sessions, with clear eligibility.
Alumni contribute back to our programmes, for example as mentors, speakers or referrers of new applicants.
We know our programme cost per enterprise supported and can show how it is calculated.
Each year our board or senior leaders approve a budget that shows income and costs by programme.
We share costs such as rent, management and shared staff across programmes using a written method.
We compare actual spending with budget at least monthly and act on large differences.
Our accounts for the last completed financial year were audited by an independent auditor.
Our accounting system records income and spending by donor fund and programme code.
No single person can approve a payment, make it and record it.
We reconcile every bank and mobile money account to the cashbook each month.
We submit donor and financial reports by the due dates set in our agreements.
Our leaders receive management accounts every month, within 15 days of month end.
We track spending against each donor's budget and eligible cost rules, so ineligible costs are found before the funder finds them.
Our unrestricted reserves can cover core running costs for at least three months.
We update a cash flow forecast for at least the next six months every month.
No single funder provided more than half of our income in the last financial year.
Part of our income is multi-year or core funding that is not tied to a single project.
We earn income from fees, services or success fees.
We do not depend mainly on unrelated consulting work to keep the organisation running.
We record each introduction we make to investors, lenders or buyers and what came of it.
Our investor and finance partners are active and suited to the stage and size of our enterprises.
We check an enterprise's records, numbers and documents with a coach before we introduce it to an investor or lender.
We check that the finance offered through our partners has clear, fair terms before we encourage enterprises to take it.
Our working partnerships with other support organisations, government bodies, banks or buyers are written down, with each partner's role.
We keep a list of expected funding opportunities for the next 12 months, with the chance of winning and a person responsible for each.
We meet each major funder at least once a year to discuss results and future plans, beyond reporting requirements.
When we agree funding, we ask for the real cost of delivery, including a fair share of running costs such as rent and management.
Our board or governing body meets regularly, with minutes and a quorum.
Board members and senior staff sign a conflict of interest declaration each year, kept in a register.
The board reviews the director's performance against agreed targets at least once a year.
We have a written plan for who would lead the organisation if the director left unexpectedly.
Our core programme staff stay long enough for the organisation to keep what it has learned.
When our own expertise is not enough, we bring in outside consultants or partners rather than promise services we cannot deliver.
Every staff member received a documented performance review in the last 12 months.
We vet mentors and coaches against written criteria, including references, before they work with entrepreneurs.
Each mentor signs a written agreement on hours, confidentiality, conduct and conflicts of interest before starting.
We review each mentor's activity and ratings from session logs at least once a year and decide whether to renew, coach or release them.
We have a written safeguarding policy, approved by our board, that covers staff, mentors, volunteers and the entrepreneurs we serve.
We run a complaints channel that entrepreneurs know about and that accepts confidential reports.
Staff and mentors complete safeguarding and code of conduct training before they work with entrepreneurs.
We keep all client enterprise records in one database, with a unique ID for each enterprise.
Applicant, participant and alumni records are linked in one system, so we can follow each enterprise from application to alumni.
Our client database has complete data on the fields we report on, such as gender, age, location, revenue and jobs.
We have a written guide that defines each data field and indicator and how it is collected.
We have defined indicators with baseline values for our entrepreneurs, such as revenue, jobs and finance accessed.
We follow up enterprises after the programme ends and collect outcome data, not only during the programme.
When we report results, we use a comparison group or state how much of the change we can and cannot attribute to our programme.
We check a sample of reported results against documents such as sales records, bank statements or payroll, not only entrepreneur statements.
Our leaders use results data to decide which programmes to continue, change or stop.
We report disappointing or negative results to our board and funders, not only successes.
After each cohort we hold a structured review with staff and entrepreneurs and record the changes we will make.
Each major programme is reviewed against relevance, effectiveness, efficiency and sustainability at least once per funding cycle.
Our organisation's legal registration and annual filings with the Registrar of Companies are up to date.
We hold a current licence as a non-profit organisation from the NPO Secretariat and renew it on time.
Our tax registration and returns with the Ghana Revenue Authority are up to date.
We remit statutory staff deductions, such as SSNIT contributions and PAYE, on time.
Our organisation is registered with the Data Protection Commission and the registration is current.
We obtain informed consent from entrepreneurs, explained in plain language, on what personal data we collect, why, and who will see it.
We protect personal data with technical and organisational security measures and have a procedure for data breaches.
We keep a risk register with owners and review it at least every quarter.
We check funders, partners and major donors before accepting money or agreements, for example their source of funds and reputation.
We verify basic facts about an enterprise, such as registration, ownership and key claims, before we endorse it or introduce it to an investor.
We have a written anti-fraud and anti-corruption policy that staff, mentors and board members have read and signed.
We buy goods and services using written procurement rules that require quotations above a set amount.
Suspected fraud or misuse of funds is recorded, investigated and reported to the board and affected funders.
Women make up a meaningful share of the people who decide which enterprises we select.
Each year we review our selection, curriculum and mentoring for barriers facing women and young people, such as timing, venue, childcare or biased scoring.
We set written targets for women and young people in each cohort and report against them.
We compare outcomes such as revenue, jobs and finance raised for women and men and for different age groups each year.
We help entrepreneurs assess the climate and environmental risks and opportunities in their businesses.
We screen enterprises we promote or link to finance for serious environmental or social harm, and decline or set conditions where we find it.
We can call on climate and environment expertise through staff, mentors or partners, such as universities or specialist agencies, when entrepreneurs need it.
We track climate or environmental results, such as the number of enterprises adopting resource efficient or climate smart practices.
We reach rural entrepreneurs through design choices such as location, language and delivery method, not only through open calls.
We know what share of our participants are based outside the regional capital and compare it with a written target or the spread of enterprises in our area.
We reduce cost and access barriers for participants, such as transport, data costs, fee waivers or accessible venues.
We share our curriculum, tools or findings with other support organisations or policy makers.
